prompt: The quota allows four pods in `team-a`. Ana scales the Deployment to six. What does `kubectl get deployment` show?

choices.why: Right: four pods admitted, two refused by the quota.

choices.text: An error, and the old count of two
choices.why: The scale itself was accepted; only pod creation was refused.

choices.text: `6/6`, since quotas are only warnings
choices.why: Quotas are enforced on every create.

choices.text: `6/6`, with two pods `Pending`
choices.why: No pod was ever created for the two extra copies.

prompt: Where did Ana find the reason the fifth and sixth pods never appeared?
hint: Who tried to create those pods?

choices.text: In the Deployment's status
choices.why: It said `4/6` and nothing more.

choices.text: In the logs of the pods that did start
choices.why: Those pods never knew about the refusal.

choices.text: In a `FailedCreate` event, recorded when the ReplicaSet was refused
choices.why: Right: `exceeded quota: team-a, requested: pods=1, used: pods=4, limited: pods=4`.

choices.text: On two pods stuck in `Pending`
choices.why: There were no such pods; the API server refused to create them.

prompt: After the refusal, the quota read `pods 4/4`, `requests.cpu 400m/1`, `requests.memory 256Mi/512Mi`. The team lowers each pod's memory request to 32Mi. Can it now run six pods?

choices.text: Yes, because memory was the problem
choices.why: Memory still had room; the pod count was full.

choices.text: Yes, because smaller pods use less of every limit
choices.why: Smaller pods still count as one pod each.

choices.text: No: the pod count is the ceiling it hit
choices.why: Right. Whichever line is reached first stops the namespace.

choices.text: No, because a quota cannot be changed once set
choices.why: A quota is an object like any other and can be edited.

prompt: `kubectl create deployment` wrote no resources, yet the pod had `requests: cpu 100m, memory 64Mi`. Where did they come from?
hint: An object in the namespace fills in what is missing.

choices.text: From the ResourceQuota, divided by the pod limit
choices.why: A quota caps totals; it never writes into a pod.

choices.text: From the LimitRange's defaults
choices.why: Right: `defaultRequest` and `default` are written into containers that left them out.

choices.text: From the image's metadata
choices.why: Images carry no resource requests.

choices.text: From the scheduler, after placing the pod
choices.why: They were set before the pod was admitted, let alone placed.

prompt: Why does a namespace with a CPU or memory quota almost always need a LimitRange too?
hint: What happens to a pod with no requests in such a namespace?

choices.text: The quota does nothing without one
choices.why: The quota capped pods on its own.

choices.text: To make pods start faster
choices.why: Defaults change admission, not start-up time.

choices.text: Because LimitRanges are required by the scheduler
choices.why: The scheduler never reads them.

choices.text: A pod without requests cannot be counted, so it is refused
choices.why: Right. The defaults turn a forgotten field into a sensible value instead of a failed deploy.

prompt: `greedy` asked for a 512Mi memory limit while the namespace still had 512Mi of limits free. Why was it refused?
hint: The message named a per-container ceiling.

choices.text: The quota had run out of memory
choices.why: It had 512Mi left, exactly what was asked.

choices.text: The LimitRange caps one container at 256Mi
choices.why: Right: `maximum memory usage per Container is 256Mi`.

choices.text: Pods may not be created directly in a namespace with a quota
choices.why: They can; this one was refused for its size.

choices.text: A limit without a request is invalid
choices.why: A request defaults to the limit when only the limit is given.
